title: Methods
text:
mcPHASES v1.0.0 on PhysioNet, restricted access under the PhysioNet Restricted Health Data License. Interval 2022: 42 participants in Toronto, about three months each, with a Fitbit Sense (nightly wrist temperature, resting heart rate, HRV, sleep breathing rate, sleep), a Dexcom G6 continuous glucose monitor, Mira urinary LH and E3G with a four-phase label per day, and a daily symptom diary on a 0–5 scale. The 2024 return interval is held out and has not been used.

title: Methods
text:
Statistics

Cohort shifts. DABEST paired mean difference and Hedges’ g with 95 % bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap intervals over participants (5,000 resamples). Native units are primary; g only to compare cells across signals.
Repeatability. Each closed cycle’s luteal − follicular shift is standardized by the pooled between-person SD of phase means. Euclidean distance between cycle vectors over their shared features, rescaled to the full dimension. Mean distance between a person’s own cycles against the mean distance to other people’s cycles, in the same participants. ICC(1) per feature from one-way ANOVA with unequal group sizes. Intervals from 5,000 participant resamples, BCa.
No hypothesis tests and no multiplicity adjustment. Every number is an estimate with an interval; counts of participants in each cell are stated.
Figures. DABEST forest plots draw each contrast’s bootstrap as a half-violin with the estimate and its 95 % BCa interval. The whorlmap draws the bootstrap of Hedges’ g inside each cell of the feature × contrast grid, the outer ring being the tail nearest zero and the centre the far tail. Colour and axis ranges are set from the plotted values so that no cell saturates, and the range is printed on the figure. Device signals are blue, symptoms orange, throughout.

title: Methods
text:
Disclosure

Every figure and table pools at least five participants; most pool 24 to 42.
No participant-level value, identifier, calendar date or free-text entry appears in this repository or on this site.
The repeatability and comparison figures are drawn from the cohort-level tables in tables/ by scripts/make_figures.py; the cohort-shift figures are the analysis run’s own, every element a cohort bootstrap. The code that reads the restricted dataset is released from a separate repository after review, as the data licence asks of code behind publications.

title: phaseffect
text:
Interval 2022 of the mcPHASES dataset: 42 participants, Fitbit Sense, Dexcom CGM, Mira urine hormones and a daily diary over about three months. Phases come from the hormone-based labels. Every contrast is within the same participants, against their own follicular days, and is reported as an effect size with a 95 % interval. Nothing on this site is participant-level.


Cohort shifts by phase
Luteal − follicular, same participants: resting heart rate +3.0 bpm [2.2, 3.8], wrist temperature +0.23 °C [0.12, 0.31], glucose +0.16 mmol/L [0.06, 0.27], breathing rate +0.48 /min, HRV −3.9 ms. Menses is the symptom phase: cramps +1.1 points, 41 of 42 participants higher.



Does a person’s shift repeat?
Yes for resting heart rate: between-person SD 1.9 bpm [0.7, 2.7] on a 3.0 bpm cohort shift; two of a person’s own cycles already outweigh the cohort mean. Barely for wrist temperature: 0.11 °C [0.04, 0.27] on a 0.28 °C shift, eleven cycles to break even. Over five signals the personal part of the shift vector is small, R_vec 0.07 [−0.11, 0.27].



Methods in one screen · Prior findings on this dataset · aggregate tables in tables/

title: Cohort shifts by phase
text: Positive means higher than on the participant’s own follicular days. Paired mean differences with 95 % bias-corrected bootstrap intervals over 5,000 participant resamples (methods). The luteal phase moves every device signal in the same participants; menses moves the symptoms.

title: Cohort shifts by phase
text:
Standardized, to compare across signals
Hedges’ g uses the spread of participants’ phase means as its unit, so a consistent 3 bpm shift against baselines that differ by 7 bpm between people scores lower than a one-point symptom shift against baselines that differ by less than a point. Use it to compare cells, not to size an effect.



Whorlmap of Hedges’ g. Each cell spirals its 5,000 bootstrap values from the tail nearest zero (outer ring) to the far tail (centre), 2.5 % trimmed at each end, so a coloured outer ring means the 95 % interval excludes zero. Colour range ±2, set by the widest cell. Rows ordered within each family by its strongest contrast.





The same g with its bootstrap as half-violins, families by contrasts. Each family row has its own scale.





Do two phase contrasts move the same features? One dot per feature. The fertile-window and luteal vectors point the same way; menses is its own direction. Descriptive: features are not independent.

title: Cohort shifts by phase
text:
Read with

Reference phase. Mira’s “Follicular” label is short (median 6 days) and excludes menses and the fertile window. Published contrasts use a late-follicular reference, so agreement with them is same-direction, not replication.
Open cycles included. Days in cycles that never closed count towards their labelled phase; a closed-cycle sensitivity run is pending.
Multiplicity. 51 cells, no adjustment. 36 exclude zero; two or three would by chance. Symptom cells are strongly correlated with each other.
Not blind. Participants saw the app’s phase predictions while reporting symptoms.
Data handling. 782 of 3,698 resting-heart-rate days were coded 0 and treated as missing; two participants’ glucose was converted from mg/dL; 16 of 3,258 temperature nights were dropped as artefacts.

Table: tables/cohort_phenovector.csv, 51 rows, no identifiers.

title: Prior findings on this dataset
text: Seventeen formal works and about twenty-five repositories touch the dataset. Everything physiological that is published is a pooled group contrast (glucose, wrist temperature, resting heart rate), a classifier score, or a symptom model. No published work reports a within-person effect with its uncertainty, a cross-signal concordance, or anything anchored on the 2024 progesterone metabolite. This page is the context for the findings here; figures reproduced from other works carry their own licence, stated in the caption.

title: Does a person’s shift repeat?
text:
Yes for resting heart rate, barely for wrist temperature. A three-level model of the daily values (person, cycle, day) splits each signal’s luteal shift into its parts. Resting heart rate: between-person SD 1.9 bpm [0.7, 2.7] on a 3.0 bpm cohort shift, repeatability 0.49 [0.09, 0.83]; two of a person’s own cycles already outweigh the cohort mean. Wrist temperature: SD 0.11 °C [0.04, 0.27] on a 0.28 °C shift, single-cycle repeatability 0.08, eleven cycles to break even. Over the five signals the personal part of the shift vector is small: R_vec 0.07 [−0.11, 0.27], 75 % of resamples positive.

title: Does a person’s shift repeat?
text:
Read with

Two or three cycles per person, 22 people for the vector; 21 to 34 with two or more cycles per signal for the model. Nothing here is a precise personal repeatability, only its presence for resting heart rate and its smallness for temperature.
Day noise dominates temperature: 71 % of a single cycle’s temperature shift is night-to-night noise in the phase means, 21 % cycle-to-cycle, 8 % the person. Glucose’s shift varies from cycle to cycle more than between people.
Sore breasts, the one symptom checked, is itself repeatable (SD 0.44 points [0.11, 0.62]); symptoms were reported while participants saw the app’s phase predictions.
Closed cycles from menstrual onsets in the labels, 10–60 days; the short “Follicular” label is the reference; nothing uses the 2024 interval.

title: Does a person’s shift repeat?
section: The earlier check: 17 features on the between-person scale
text:
The earlier check: 17 features on the between-person scale
Before the model above, a cruder check put all 17 features (six device signals and eleven symptoms) on a common scale, the between-person spread of phase means, and asked whether a person’s cycle vectors lie closer to each other than to other people’s. They did not: ratio 1.00 [0.92, 1.08] over 24 participants. On that scale a consistent 3 bpm shift against baselines that differ by 7 bpm between people counts for less than a one-point symptom shift, and the symptom noise swamps the device signals. Per feature, resting heart rate was already the one repeatable signal (ICC 0.61 [0.09, 0.86], 14 participants) and temperature already was not (−0.02 [−0.34, 0.31]).



Left: mean distance between a person’s own cycle vectors and to other people’s, 17 features. Right: per-feature ICC of the shift across a person’s cycles.


Tables: tables/rep03_components.csv, tables/rep03_design_curve.csv, tables/rep03_summary.json; the earlier check’s tables/feature_icc.csv and tables/repeatability_summary.json.
